entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Khālid ibn ʿAbd al‐Malik al‐Marwarrūdhī, a distinguished astronomer of the early 9th century CE, played a pivotal role in the scientific renaissance of the Abbasid Caliphate. Operating primarily from Baghdad, the intellectual heart of the Islamic world, Khālid was a key figure in the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Ḥikmah) under the patronage of Caliph al-Maʾmūn (reigned 813–833 CE). His contributions centered on refining astronomical observations and calculations, building upon the rich legacies of Hellenistic and Indian scientific traditions, and pushing the boundaries of geodesy during a period of intense scholarly inquiry.

Among Khālid's most significant achievements was his participation in the ambitious project to measure the Earth's circumference, known as the Maʾmūnic arc measurement, around 827 CE. This endeavor involved two teams of astronomers and geographers, one working from Tadmur (Palmyra) northward and another from Baghdad southward, to measure the length of one degree of latitude. Khālid was instrumental in the southern expedition, which yielded a result remarkably close to modern values (approximately 111.8 km per degree compared to the actual 111.1 km). He also compiled important astronomical tables (zijes) and made precise observations of celestial bodies, including solar and lunar eclipses, which were crucial for refining existing planetary models and developing more accurate calendars.

entities.summary:
Khālid ibn ʿAbd al‐Malik al‐Marwarrūdhī was a preeminent astronomer and geographer of the early 9th century CE, instrumental in the scientific blossoming of the Abbasid Caliphate under Caliph al-Ma'mun. His contributions were central to the House of Wisdom's ambitious projects to refine astronomical observations and establish the Earth's dimensions, marking a significant advancement in Islamic science and globally. He is particularly renowned for his role in the first direct measurement of the Earth's circumference by Islamic scholars, a feat that combined theoretical knowledge with practical, large-scale surveying.

Working within the vibrant intellectual environment of Baghdad, Khālid ibn ʿAbd al‐Malik participated in two groundbreaking expeditions commissioned by Caliph al-Ma'mun around 827 CE. One team traveled north from Tadmur (Palmyra) toward Raqqa, while another measured south from Kufa, aiming to determine the length of a degree of latitude. By meticulously measuring the distance between two points where the elevation of the celestial pole differed by one degree, they derived a value for the Earth's circumference that was remarkably close to modern estimates, ranging from 24,000 to 25,000 miles. Beyond geodesy, al-Marwarrūdhī also contributed to the development of astronomical instruments and the compilation of *zij* tables, which provided essential data for celestial calculations.

The meticulous work of al-Marwarrūdhī and his contemporaries profoundly influenced subsequent Islamic and European scientific thought. Their empirical approach to geodesy and astronomy laid foundational groundwork for later cartography and navigation, demonstrating the practical application of Greek mathematical traditions combined with innovative observational techniques. The precision achieved in measuring the Earth's circumference stood as a testament to the scientific rigor of the Abbasid era, inspiring generations of scholars and explorers.

His work significantly contributed to the empirical foundation of astronomy and geodesy, impacting subsequent cartography and scientific inquiry for centuries.
